What I admire most about those who lead a country is not the position they hold, but the responsibility they carry. Making consequential decisions, often under immense pressure, while balancing competing national priorities is an extraordinary test of leadership.

That is why meeting a former head of state is always a special experience for me.

At the recent Confederation of Indian Industry interaction with CAF -banco de desarrollo de América Latina y el Caribe-, the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, I had the privilege of meeting H.E. Eduardo Frei Ruiz-Tagle, former President of Chile, alongside H.E. Sergio Díaz Granados Guida, Executive President of CAF, H.E. Janaina Tewaney Mencomo, former Foreign Minister of Panama, and distinguished diplomatic representatives from across the region.

Latin America also holds a very personal place in my life. Being married to a Nicaraguan, I consider the region family. It was particularly meaningful to learn more about the remarkable work underway across its economies, industries and institutions, and the role CII is playing in bringing our regions closer.

One message I emphasized during my industry intervention was that India and Latin America have an opportunity to build something far more substantial than a traditional trading relationship.

Consider critical minerals. Latin America has significant mineral resources, while India brings industrial capabilities, a growing technology ecosystem and demand for strategic materials. 

Why not combine these strengths through joint ventures in mineral extraction and processing, collaborative research between universities and industry, and partnerships that develop technologies and create value in both regions?

It is encouraging to see the Government of India giving greater priority to its relationship with Latin America. The growing engagement at the highest levels presents a real opportunity for Indian industry.

I have always felt that there is tremendous goodwill towards India across Latin America. But goodwill alone does not create economic partnerships. It needs to be translated into investment, research collaboration, technology deployment and projects on the ground.

The next chapter of India–Latin America relations should not be measured only by diplomatic engagements and agreements signed, but by the industries we build, the technologies we develop and the opportunities we create together.

My sincere thanks to Renni B. and the entire Confederation of Indian Industry team for organizing this meaningful interaction and giving me the opportunity to contribute an industry perspective.

Goldman, Citi lead 21-bank group backing stablecoin with $270M

The venture builds on an initiative announced in October 2025, when ten international banks began exploring the development of digital money backed one-to-one by reserve assets and available on public blockchains. 

Banking Consortium Targets $293 Billion Stablecoin Market

By September 2026, the group had expanded to 21 institutions and formally announced plans to establish a dedicated stablecoin company. Participating organizations include Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup, Fidelity Investments, Capital One, PNC Financial Services, UBS, Banco Santander, Deutsche Bank, Lloyds Banking Group and MUFG Bank. Other members include BBVA, Commerzbank, Crédit Agricole, Rabobank, TD Bank, Scotiabank, WisdomTree, Standard Bank and Sirius International Holding.


Project Faro Brings Together 21 Global Financial Institutions
Project Faro enters a market dominated by Tether and Circle, whose USDT and USDC stablecoins collectively account for approximately 84% of the $293 billion dollar-pegged stablecoin market. As of November 10, USDT had approximately $176  billion in circulation, while USDC accounted for around $70 billion, according to DefiLlama-based market data. The consortium’s entry could introduce competition in institutional payments, particularly among businesses already using participating banks for treasury management and international settlements. Regulatory developments have also strengthened interest in bank-issued stablecoins.

Momentum 

The U.S. GENIUS Act, signed into law in July 2025, established a federal framework covering reserve backing, redemption rights and oversight of payment stablecoin issuers. On October 21, 2026, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finalized implementing regulations scheduled to take effect on January 18, 2027.  

▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

Why now? The commitment turns September's 21-institution announcement into a funded buildout, timed to a new US regulatory framework. The GENIUS Act, which governs stablecoins, is due to take effect in January 2027.

What's the endgame? The venture remains pre-launch. It is seeking a chief executive officer and targeting the first half of 2027 for a dollar stablecoin, with a euro version planned later.

What could go wrong? Competition is already substantial. USDT and USDC dominate the market, and other bank and payments-industry groups are developing rival stablecoin or settlement initiatives. The funding alone does not establish that the venture can win users or compete with established issuers.

Bottonline  The consortium's scale and potential bank distribution make it a serious bid to bring regulated digital money into payments and settlement. It is a sign that incumbent lenders now see stablecoins as infrastructure worth building together rather than ceding to crypto-native firms.

3 analyst questions from Maruti's Q2 FY2027 earnings call that caught my attention.

I have analysed Maruti Suzuki's latest FY2027 Q2 earnings call.

Among all the discussions and responses between management and analysts, 3 questions caught my attention the most.

The first question was raised by Gunjan Prithyani from Bank of America.

In her question, she raised the issue of the company's pricing actions being very modest despite strong demand and commodity cost pressure.

She also asked about near-term margin performance in relation to the parent company's 10% medium-term EBIT guidance and the company's margin tolerance if margins remained at current levels.

Management replied that demand is strong and that they will find opportunities to recover margins.

They also mentioned that the steel industry is asking for high prices by taking advantage of the current situation.

From this question, I got a better understanding of management's take on margin recovery, its outlook on margins and commodity costs.

Coming to the 2nd question,

It was asked by Kumar Rakesh from BNP Paribas.

His question was about the fixed-cost incidence benefit the company had recently received.

He expected that this benefit might turn into a headwind in Q3, due to lower production than wholesale dispatches expected during that period.

He also raised concerns about gross margins.

Management replied that demand is still strong and that they have to cater to the leftover 2,70,000 pending orders in the coming quarter.

However, there are still factors such as commodity cost movements and many other factors to consider before talking about gross margins.

I found this question insightful because it shifted the discussion from the company's Q2 margin performance to the sustainability of those margins in the coming quarter.

And the last interesting question was asked by Chandramouli Muthiah from Goldman Sachs.

Management had said that small-car demand had started to increase after the GST rate cut.

He raised a question about this statement and expressed concern about why the company's S-Presso still had lower dispatches compared to its usual quarterly volumes.

He also referred to the discontinuation of the Ignis.

I found this question interesting because it challenged management's statement about the recovery in small-car demand.

Despite management's positive outlook, the lower dispatches of the S-Presso raised questions about whether the recovery was actually visible across all small-car models.

Also, management didn't give a direct answer to this concern, which made me more curious about the company's small-car strategy.

The AI race has a new bottleneck. It is not chips. It is power. The organisations that map this constraint early will define the next phase of the buildout. Those that discover it late will be defined by it. Three structural shifts explain why. (Read Benori's full analysis: https://lnkd.in/gdNmNRDn).

1) Supply cannot keep pace with demand. Global data centre power demand has risen 27% in 2026 alone (reaching 132 gigawatts). Bank of America estimates data centres will add 125 gigawatts of US electric load by 2030. Regulated utilities are on track to supply less than half. Large gas turbines, the fastest conventional solution, are sold out through 2030.

2) Power is now a diligence variable. Grid access, interconnection queue position, and permitting timelines are as material to an AI investment thesis as technology or customer contracts are. Yet, these rarely appear in public filings. A well-located site is a stranded asset if it sits years back in a utility’s queue.

3) Second-order winners are emerging. Turbine and grid equipment manufacturers sit in a seller’s market. Battery storage and on-site generation providers are bets on bridging the gap. The chip shortage taught markets to price semiconductor exposure into every AI thesis. Power demands the same discipline.

Buffett left. His successor just spent a record ₹90,200 crore buying Berkshire's own shares — while sitting on the biggest cash pile in corporate history.

On Saturday 7 November, Berkshire reported its first full quarter under chief executive Greg Abel, who succeeded Warren Buffett this year. Operating earnings fell 5.8% to about ₹1.19 lakh crore ($12.7 billion, approx). Net profit fell 28% to about ₹2.08 lakh crore ($22.1 billion, approx). Cash hit a record ₹35.5 lakh crore ($377.4 billion, approx).

In the same quarter, Berkshire bought back about ₹90,200 crore ($9.6 billion, approx) of its own stock — a single-quarter record, more than double Q2's ₹42,300 crore. Total buybacks in 2026: about ₹1.35 lakh crore ($14.4 billion, approx).

The market has already delivered its verdict. Berkshire's B shares closed at record highs on four straight days in the week ended 13 November, taking the fourth-quarter gain to 19.1% while the broader market slipped. A month earlier it trailed the S&P 500 by 13.6 points for the year; now it leads by 5.8.

The decision: buy back a record amount of your own stock while sitting on record cash and holding a losing AI bet. Is it a vote of confidence that Berkshire is cheap — or an admission that ₹35.5 lakh crore in cash cannot find anything better to buy? Abel bought back stock and sold other equities in the same quarter. He is choosing Berkshire over the market.

The bet is Alphabet. Berkshire added about ₹94,000 crore ($10 billion, approx) in June 2026. Both classes have since fallen about 20%, cutting it to roughly ₹76,100 crore ($8.1 billion, approx). Alphabet burned about ₹85,500 crore ($9.1 billion, approx) in cash in Q3, even as revenue rose 25% and cloud revenue jumped 103%.

The filing that answers the open question lands today: Berkshire's Q3 13F will show the 30 September Alphabet share count. Barron's suggests Abel may have added to Alphabet — and trimmed Bank of America for a ninth straight quarter, by an estimated 30 to 40 million shares.

Two honest notes. The 28% profit drop is mostly unrealised investment swings — operating profit fell only 5.8%. And the cash figure depends on the definition: the headline ₹35.5 lakh crore includes railroad and utility cash; the narrower ₹3.31 lakh crore actually fell quarter on quarter.

A buyback shrinks the shares outstanding, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice of the same railroads, insurers and energy businesses. But concentration cuts both ways: five holdings — Alphabet, American Express, Apple, Bank of America and Coca-Cola — are roughly 65% of the portfolio. One position moves the whole result.

What does it tell you when a company with the biggest cash pile in corporate history decides its own stock is the best thing to buy?

Figures: Berkshire Q3 2026 release and 10-Q, 7 Nov 2026; CNBC; Barron's. $ conversions at ₹94 per $1, checked 16 Nov 2026, approximate.

Google just lost half a trillion dollars.
In one day.
Nobody hacked it. No scandal. No product failure.

Just you, saying “let me ask AI” instead of “let me Google it.”
Thursday, Alphabet Inc. stock fell nearly 13%.
About $500 billion, gone.
Its worst day ever.

For 20 years, Google was the perfect business.
Almost a monopoly. Low costs. Huge margins. Cash flowing in forever.
Investors called it the best business model on earth.

Now look at what changed.
Search growth slowed.
And Google is burning cash on AI data centres, with free cash flow turning negative.
Spending this year: about $200 billion.
Bank of America now values Google’s search business at 10x earnings. That’s cheaper than energy stocks.

Here’s the scary part.
AI infrastructure is expensive, crowded, and nobody has a monopoly on it.
So Google has to leave its best business for a much harder one.
And it doesn’t have a choice.

Google isn’t dying tomorrow.
But three years ago, “Google it” was a habit nobody questioned.
Habits are the most valuable thing a company can own.
And they’re also the easiest thing to lose.

Is this Google’s Nokia moment, or just an expensive transition?

Major US banks are now blocking AI agents that log into customer accounts using the customer's own username and password. 🏦🤖
What's going on:

→ JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo have made it clear that customers are responsible if an agent they gave their login to does something unwanted

→ The CFPB's Section 1033 rule was meant to replace password-sharing with secure data access, but a federal court has blocked enforcement

→ Most banks are moving toward read-only access for agents, so they can view but not move money

→ Bank of America, BBVA, Synchrony and Wells Fargo have joined the Personal Agent Protocol, a shared standard for how agents identify themselves

The debate: banks say it's about risk. Some critics ask if it's also about protecting deposits.
As someone learning to build AI-powered applications, this matters. Agents that touch money need identity, permissions and trust built in from day one.

DTCC’s Tokenization Service went live this week. Twenty participants, including J.P. Morgan, Citi, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Citadel Securities.

The headline is that the depository itself is now issuing tokenised entitlements — same ownership rights, same CUSIP as the conventional holding. That is a significant moment and it deserves the attention it is getting.


Settlement arrangements are left to participants for now.

The asset leg has shipped. The cash leg has not.

I have been saying for a while that most tokenisation efforts stall on the cash leg, and that it is usually treated as somebody else’s problem. Here it is at the most sophisticated post-trade infrastructure in the world, stated openly.

And there is a deeper reason it is hard, which I think is underappreciated.

NSCC netting currently reduces conventional settlement obligations by roughly 98 percent.
Atomic on-chain settlement is gross settlement. Every trade settles in full, individually.

So moving to atomic DvP means giving up almost all of that netting efficiency, unless you rebuild netting on-chain. That is not a minor engineering detail. For a market of this size it is the whole economics of settlement.

To their credit, DTCC’s roadmap includes exactly that — on-chain cash netting, alongside exploration of stablecoins and tokenised deposits. J.P. Morgan is planning JPM Coin on Canton. A Collateral AppChain is expected early next year.

The other numbers worth noting:

🔹 34 securities eligible at launch, against a No-Action Letter universe of roughly $30 trillion held at DTC
🔹 24/7 transfer works within a single chain; cross-chain conversion runs on US business hours
🔹 Transfers limited to registered wallets
🔹 BNY, the largest custodian, and Goldman are absent from the launch list


The India comparison is interesting here, and I say this carefully.

Our tokenised bond work pairs the asset leg with wholesale CBDC from the outset. The cash leg is in the design rather than deferred to participants.

Different sequencing, same destination. Neither approach is obviously right — one gets to market faster, the other solves the harder problem first.

Asset Leg → Cash Leg → Netting → Real Settlement

DTCC has shipped the first. The rest is the interesting part.

#Bankers_love_AI_until_AI_starts_loving_your_money

On 8th September 2026, Meta launched Muse — its autonomous personal AI agent. It’s less than two months old and already making bankers nervous.

Muse doesn't just answer questions. It does complex, multi-step work — research, travel planning, tracking goals, reading and generating files, shopping.

And it does one more interesting thing: with your permission, it can log into your accounts and transact across apps and websites on your behalf.

So if you tell it, "optimise my returns," it will do what any good intern would do — look at that large, idle cash lying in your bank earning next to nothing, and move it to a higher-yielding option. Example - it will move money in your saving bank account, earning 2.50% p.a. to an easy-to-break fixed deposit offering 6.50% p.a. and in the same bank.

Great for you. Terrible for your bank.

Let me tell you a secret. Banks actually love you more for the idle money that you park there, than for your life insurance purchases through them. That is why every bank proudly reports its CASA — Current Account and Savings Account — ratio. The higher the CASA, the cheaper the cost of funds, the better the Net Interest Margin, fatter the profit, more bonuses for bankers and happier shareholders. 

So a product that benefits the banking customer, immediately became a red flag for the banking chief.

In the US, banks including JPMorgan Chase, Citigroup, Bank of America and Charles Schwab have all scrambled to restrict third-party AI agents from accessing client accounts.

The language is couched in comforting phrase of "customer protection." Citigroup, for example, allows limited read-only access but does not permit agents to log in or transact directly, saying it is designed to safeguard customer accounts and information. Bank of America says it wants a human in the loop before money leaves.

And they say this with a perfectly straight face, while in the same analyst calls they sing hosannas about what AI is doing for them — productivity gains, staff reduction, cost savings.

This looks like complete hypocrisy to me — protecting lazy banking profits in the guise of customer protection, while using AI tools themselves to boost their own bottom line.

A few weeks ago, I shared this news with a few senior bankers for their opinion.

The most honest response came from a very experienced, retired banker from Kotak Mahindra Bank. He truly deserves the last word:

The banker cheers the robot's grace,
When cutting staff and leasing space. "Efficiency!" the boardroom cries,
As AI lifts the bottom line.

But if your bot should wake and say,
"This interest rate is trash, let's stray,"
The banker gasps and pulls the plug:
"For your protection," mutters, smug.

DTCC's Tokenization Service went live on 28 October, and the most important feature is what did not change: the token is the same legal position, held in the same name, at the same depository.

DTC, the DTCC subsidiary that holds more than $114 trillion in custody, now lets 20 signed-up participants convert supported securities into tokens and back. The list includes J.P. Morgan, Bank of America, Citi, Fidelity, Barclays and Citadel Securities. Supported assets are Russell 1000 stocks, ETFs tracking major indices and US Treasuries, under an SEC no-action letter from December 2025.

Here is how it works in plain terms. The token is a digital twin of a position DTC already holds. Per Morgan Lewis, as reported by Genfinity, tokenised securities stay registered to DTC's nominee, Cede & Co, which keeps the protections of Article 8 of the US Uniform Commercial Code, the law that governs how securities are held and transferred. The holder gets the same ownership rights and entitlements, plus the option to move the token to a digital wallet.

Two limits. Only DTC participants can request tokenisation, so an issuer or an end investor cannot do it directly. And the SEC letter is specific to DTC: it does not create a general framework for tokenised securities or extend relief to other firms.

The live chains are Canton, a public network, and DTCC's own private Besu network. Stellar is on the roadmap for the first half of 2027.

My read: this is the template most banks will copy. Keep the legal record where it is, tokenise the representation, and let the market decide how much it wants to move. It is slower than the crypto version of tokenisation, and that is exactly why a risk committee can sign it off. I have not seen volume figures, so nothing yet says how much of that $114 trillion will ever move.

Capital markets has moved elsewhere: Canton, live on mainnet since July 2024, has assembled a participant list — Goldman Sachs, Deutsche Bank, BNP Paribas, HSBC, Cboe, DTCC, Northern Trust, Citi, with Visa as a super validator — that first-generation platforms did not reach, and reports processing at $1.5T monthly scale.

Gold at $3,250/oz,  ₹98,000 per 10 grams?
Gold is falling despite high geopolitical and nuclear tensions because inflation fears, surging oil prices, and expectations of higher U.S. interest rates are currently overpowering its traditional safe-haven appeal. 
1. The headline that caught my eye
Bank of America's scenario: gold at $3,250/oz. Translated to Indian retail terms, that's roughly ₹98,000 per 10 grams, a level most buyers haven't seen in a long time . From the record highs earlier this year at $5,600/oz, that's a meaningful correction. And it raises an uncomfortable question about investor behavior.
2. The love affair with rising prices
When gold was climbing, everyone wanted in. FOMO drove record ETF inflows, jewellery buying, and endless "should I buy gold?" conversations. Rising prices validated the decision to buy. The narrative wrote itself.
3. The silence when prices fall
Now that a 20–25% correction is on the table, the same enthusiasm vanishes. Data from India shows this clearly: despite prices falling sharply from record highs, retail demand dropped over 70% at one point, with households selling old jewellery rather than buying fresh . Even major jewellers are holding back purchases ahead of Diwali, waiting for lower levels .
4. The "waiting to buy" paradox
Everyone says they'll buy on dips. But when the dip actually arrives, the psychology shifts. "Maybe it'll fall further." "Let me wait for the bottom." The discipline to execute a pre-planned purchase evaporates when the market is falling and headlines are negative.
5. BofA's actual stance is more nuanced
Interestingly, BofA isn't bearish. The bank suggests buying into weakness, with a range of $3,450–$3,250 as a potential accumulation zone, while still forecasting $6,000 by 2027 . 
6. The uncomfortable truth for long-term investors
Gold's role in a portfolio isn't to go up in a straight line. It's a hedge, a diversifier, a store of value over time.

Key Reasons Gold is Dropping
Surging Oil Prices & Inflation Fears: Escalating conflicts in the Middle East have driven crude oil prices above $110 a barrel. Higher energy costs threaten to reignite global inflation.
Federal Reserve Rate Expectations: Because inflation fears are rising, traders expect the U.S. Federal Reserve to keep interest rates high, or even raise them, rather than cutting them
Liquidity-Driven Selloffs & Margin Calls: During sharp market drops across equities and tech sectors, investors and institutions sometimes face cash crunches or need to cover margin calls. This forces a "flush" where even safe-haven assets like gold and silver are sold off to raise immediate cash. 
Technical Support Breaks
Strength in the U.S. Dollar
7. My takeaway
A ₹98,000/10g scenario is a stress test of conviction, not a prediction. The real question isn't whether gold will fall that far. It's whether you'd actually press the buy button if it did, or find another reason to wait.
